learningObjectives: Identify threshold, depolarisation, repolarisation and after-hyperpolarisation.
Distinguish absolute from relative refractory periods.
Relate firing patterns to neural coding and clinical excitability.

anatomy.label: Threshold
anatomy.detail: Threshold is the membrane voltage at which inward sodium current becomes self-amplifying and an action potential is initiated.
anatomy.clinical: Threshold is dynamic and shifts with recent activity, neuromodulation and channel state.

anatomy.label: Voltage-gated sodium channels
anatomy.detail: Sodium channels open quickly with depolarisation, then inactivate even while the membrane remains depolarised.
anatomy.clinical: Sodium-channel blockers can reduce pathological high-frequency firing.

anatomy.label: Voltage-gated potassium channels
anatomy.detail: Potassium channels open more slowly, allowing potassium efflux that returns voltage toward baseline.
anatomy.clinical: Altered potassium conductance can prolong spikes or destabilise firing.

anatomy.label: Refractory periods
anatomy.detail: During the absolute refractory period most sodium channels are inactivated; during the relative period stronger input may still trigger firing.
anatomy.clinical: Refractoriness limits firing rate and helps action potentials travel in one direction.

interaction.title: Action Potentials sequence
interaction.instruction: Select a component, then run the sequence to see how the system changes over time.

stages.label: Threshold
stages.text: Summed input depolarises the axon initial segment to threshold.

stages.label: Upstroke
stages.text: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium enters rapidly.

stages.label: Repolarise
stages.text: Sodium channels inactivate while potassium channels open.

stages.label: Recover
stages.text: After-hyperpolarisation and channel recovery restore readiness.

quizBank.question: What directly produces the rapid upstroke of an action potential?
quizBank.explanation: Rapid sodium influx drives the depolarising upstroke.

quizBank.question: Why does an action potential not normally travel backward?
quizBank.explanation: The refractory region behind the spike cannot immediately regenerate another action potential.

quizBank.question: What ends the sodium current during the spike?
quizBank.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels rapidly enter an inactivated state.

quizBank.question: During the relative refractory period:
options: A stronger-than-usual input may trigger another spike
No spike is possible under any condition
The neuron has no membrane voltage
All potassium channels are permanently closed
quizBank.explanation: Residual potassium conductance means stronger depolarisation is needed.

quizBank.question: Action-potential amplitude usually encodes stimulus strength by:
options: It generally does not; rate and timing carry more information
Growing larger with every stronger stimulus
quizBank.explanation: Individual spikes are stereotyped; firing pattern conveys intensity and context.
